subject: physics
title: Forces and elasticity
key_idea: Stretching, bending or compressing an object needs more than one force. For a spring, force is directly proportional to extension until the limit of proportionality (Hooke's law). The work done on the spring is stored as elastic potential energy.

sections.heading: Changing the shape of an object

blocks.text: Forces can stretch, bend or compress an object. This section covers what is needed and what happens when the force is removed.

items: To change the shape of an object, **two or more forces** must act on it, in different directions.
Stretching is an example: the forces pull in opposite directions. Compressing is the same idea, with the forces pushing in.
Fixing one end of an object counts as the second force.
This applies to stationary objects, such as a spring held in a clamp.

items.meaning: The object returns to its original shape or length when the force is removed.
The object does not return to its original shape or length when the force is removed.
The increase in length of a spring: extended length minus original length.

items: Changing shape needs two or more forces.
An elastic object returns to its original shape.
An inelastically deformed object stays changed.

blocks.text: For a spring, the extension is directly proportional to the force, provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.

blocks.label: Force on a spring
where: k is the spring constant in newtons per metre (N/m).
e is extension in metres (m). The same equation works for compression, where e is the compression.

items.text: A spring extends by 1.50 cm: e = 0.015 m.

diagram.alt: Calculate the force needed to stretch a spring of a given spring constant by a given extension in centimetres. New numbers each time.
diagram.question: A spring has a spring constant of {k} N/m. Calculate the force needed to extend it by {e} cm.
working: Convert the extension to metres: {e} cm ÷ 100

items: A **linear** relationship gives a straight line through the origin. Force and extension are directly proportional.
A **non-linear** relationship gives a curve. The extension is no longer proportional to the force.
A spring is linear up to its limit of proportionality, then the line curves.
In the linear part, the spring constant is the force divided by the extension.
Beyond the elastic limit, the spring is inelastically deformed and does not return to its original length.
A spring with a low spring constant is easy to stretch: a given force gives a large extension.

blocks.label: Spring constant (linear part)
where: k is the spring constant in newtons per metre (N/m).

items: F = k × e, with the extension in metres.
Convert centimetres or millimetres to metres first.
Beyond the limit of proportionality the relationship is non-linear.

blocks.text: A force that stretches or compresses a spring does work. Provided the spring is not inelastically deformed, the work done equals the elastic potential energy stored.

blocks.label: Elastic potential energy
where: Ee is elastic potential energy in joules (J). It is the same as the work done in stretching.
k is the spring constant in newtons per metre (N/m).
e is extension in metres (m). It is squared.

items.text: A spring with k = 8500 N/m is compressed by 1.2 cm: e = 0.012 m.

diagram.alt: Change the spring constant and the extension and see the force and the energy stored.

blocks.text: Doubling the extension doubles the force but makes the stored energy four times bigger, because the extension is squared.

items: Ee = ½ × k × e². The extension is squared.
The work done equals the energy stored, up to the limit of proportionality.

checks.q: Describe the difference between elastic deformation and inelastic deformation.
checks.a: An elastically deformed object returns to its original shape or length when the force is removed. An inelastically deformed object does not.

checks.q: A force of 4.0 N gives an extension of 0.064 m. Calculate the spring constant.
A spring with a spring constant of 30 N/m is stretched by 4.0 cm. Calculate the energy transferred.

exam_phrases: will return to its original shape / length when the force is removed
will not go back to its original length when the force is removed
the extension is no longer proportional to the force
springs with a low spring constant can compress by a larger amount
the spring has reached its limit of proportionality

mistakes.wrong: k = 2.88 ÷ 1.50 = 1.92 N/m, using the extension in centimetres.
mistakes.right: The conversion is worth a mark of its own. 1.50 cm = 0.015 m, so k = 2.88 ÷ 0.015 = 192 N/m.

mistakes.wrong: A soft mattress needs springs with a high spring constant.
mistakes.right: A soft mattress needs springs with a low spring constant, because they can compress by a larger amount for a given force.

mistakes.wrong: An object that is inelastically deformed returns to its original shape.
mistakes.right: It will not go back to its original length (or shape) when the force is removed.

worked_example.question: A door is fitted with a lock. The lock contains a spring. When the door unlocks, a force of 2.88 N is applied to the spring. The spring extends by 1.50 cm. Calculate the spring constant of the spring.
worked_example.tip: One mark each for converting, substituting, rearranging and the answer. Without the conversion, the later method marks can still be awarded.

exam_phrases: idea of keeping below the elastic limit

mistakes.wrong: The work done is ½ × 20 × 9² = 810 J for an extension of 0.09 m.
mistakes.right: The extension must be in metres: ½ × 20 × 0.09² = 0.081 J. The unconverted answer earns only one mark.

mistakes.wrong: k = 0.50 ÷ 0.013² = 2958 N/m for a force of 0.50 N and an extension of 13 mm.
mistakes.right: Do not square the extension when using force and extension. Use k = F ÷ e = 0.50 ÷ 0.013 = 38 N/m. The squared version earns only 1 mark.

worked_example.question: A spring has a spring constant of 250 N/m. Calculate the work done in stretching the spring by 0.30 m. State the unit. Use the equation E = ½ × k × x².
worked_example.tip: The unit is an independent mark. No power of ten errors are allowed in the evaluation.

exam_phrases: two (or more) forces acting in different directions
plastic: stays deformed when the force is removed
elastic: returns to original shape when the force is removed
force and extension relationship is no longer linear

mistakes.wrong: To change the shape of an object you need to apply one force.
mistakes.right: Two or more forces are needed, acting in different directions. A fixed end of the material counts as the second force.

mistakes.wrong: Plastic deformation means the object returns to its original shape.
mistakes.right: Plastic: it stays deformed when the force is removed. Elastic: it returns to its original shape.

mistakes.wrong: A spring has an original length of 3.0 cm and an extended length of 7.0 cm, so the extension is 7.0 cm.
mistakes.right: Extension = extended length − original length = 4.0 cm. Using the wrong data point loses the substitution mark.

worked_example.question: A climber investigates how a rope stretches with different forces. The results: force 0 N, 10 N, 20 N, 30 N, 40 N gives extension 0.00 m, 0.15 m, 0.3 m, 0.45 m, 0.60 m. Calculate the spring constant for the rope. Give your answer to two significant figures. Use the equation: force = extension × spring constant.
answer_points: Substitute any pair of values from the table: 40 / 0.6
worked_example.tip: Any two matching values from the table can be used. The final mark is for rounding to 2 significant figures.
